newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. says China needs new offers to win WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says China needs new offers to win WTO entry.

text.p: The United States said on Monday that China must try harder if it is to succeed in its bid for much-coveted membership of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"There has been general agreement in Geneva that China's offers are not adequate and do not form an adequate basis on which to undertake a serious negotiation," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told a news conference at the WTO's first ministerial meeting.
"That being the case, China needs to make a renewed effort with respect to WTO accession. That's not something that other countries can do for them," she said.
European Union officials have said they would like to discuss China's WTO accession with the United States, Japan and Canada at a luncheon scheduled for Tuesday.
Barshefsky said she did not know what specific proposals EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan had in mind on China's accession.
But Brittan said earlier on Monday that an effort to re-launch an earnest negotiation on China's membership of the world trade body was a key objective for him at this week's meeting in Singapore.
The European Union (EU) was trying to bring the United States on board regarding its proposal that China enter the world trade body through a phased accession process, one EU official said.
Brittan has visited China several times in recent months and has said he has received a warm response from Beijing to a proposal to stagger its accession to the 128-member WTO.
The United States has said it wants China in the WTO, but only on a commercially acceptable basis.

U.S. officials have said, though, that they are willing to be flexible on some issues but insist Beijing must comply with most of a "road map" to open its markets and eliminate trade and non-trade barriers before it can win U.S. support for its entry.
China had hoped to culminate its decade-long bid to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade by becoming a founding member of the WTO at its inception two years ago.
Its application foundered on opposition over entry terms, with Beijing maintaining that the price of the road map was too high. Talks continue at a snail's pace in Geneva.

One aim of Tuesday's luncheon would be to try to narrow differences between the United States and Europe over terms for China's entry, terms used by Beijing to play one side off against the other, one EU source said.
Brittan signalled his attitude to ministers at the conference opening session.

"We have the remarkable changes going on in China, as well as a continuing process of economic renewal elsewhere in Asia and in Latin America...Hence the urgent need for WTO enlargement," Brittan said.

In his inaugural address to the conference, Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong also backed China's entry in a reference to pending memberships, although he repeated the United States stand that new applicants must meet the necessary criteria.
Senior Chinese analyst Pei Changhong said last week China was unlikely to concede on its demand to enter as a developing country and has the patience to wait for accession on its terms.
The United States insists that the size of China's economy ranks it as a developed country.
A goal of 1997 entry seemed an ambitious target given the distance between the United States and China on so many issues, but Pei said he hoped to see entry by 1999.
China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said last month that talks with the United States on entry could be wrapped up by mid-1997.
